# Pan-African Banking Integration Strategy: Multi-Country Acquisition Consolidation

## Executive Summary

A pan-African banking group acquiring banks in Nigeria, Kenya, and Morocco faces a **regulatory trilemma**: (1) Group headquarters demands speed-to-synergy (cost reduction, unified products), (2) national regulators demand local continuity and sovereignty (separate balance sheets, local boards), and (3) customers/local management demand continuity (familiar brands, local decision-making). **Simultaneous integration fails** because it violates regulatory red lines and triggers management defection.

**Core Challenge:** Each acquired bank operates under a distinct regulatory regime with non-negotiable sovereignty requirements:
- **Nigeria (CBN):** Require local majority ownership; prohibit consolidated balance sheet; demand Nigerian board majority; control FX operations locally
- **Kenya (CBK):** Allow foreign ownership but require independent subsidiary structure; demand local MD; control credit policy locally
- **Morocco (Bank Al-Maghrib, BAM):** Require Moroccan majority ownership (51%+ local); mandate local board control; separate capital adequacy standards

**A "Fast Integration" approach (one global system, one brand, centralized decision-making) will fail** because:
1. **Regulators will block or delay approvals** (violating sovereignty)
2. **Local management will leave en masse** (loss of institutional knowledge, customer relationships)
3. **Customers will churn** (brand loyalty loss, perceived foreign control)
4. **Cost savings don't materialize** (chaos, rework, regulation fines)

**Solution Framework: "Integrated Autonomy"** — Design a phased approach where each subsidiary maintains **regulatory and operational independence** while capturing **synergies in non-regulated areas** (technology infrastructure, back-office automation, talent development, procurement). Sequence by regulatory risk and customer impact, not corporate convenience.

---

## Part I: Regulatory & Competitive Context

### A. Regulatory Reality in Each Market

#### **Nigeria (Central Bank of Nigeria—CBN)**

```
REGULATORY CONSTRAINTS (Non-Negotiable)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Ownership Structure:                                          │
│ ├─ Foreign ownership: Maximum 60% (CBN directive 2023)        │
│ ├─ Local ownership: Minimum 40% (must include Nigerians)      │
│ ├─ Board composition: Minimum 40% Nigerian citizens           │
│ ├─ Consequence: CANNOT consolidate into parent balance sheet  │
│ └─ Status: Likely to remain separate subsidiary indefinitely  │
│                                                               │
│ Management Control:                                          │
│ ├─ Managing Director: Must be Nigerian national               │
│ ├─ Chief Risk Officer: CBN audits; must answer to CBN         │
│ ├─ Board majority: Nigerian nationals (40%+ rule applies)     │
│ ├─ Implication: Day-to-day decisions made locally             │
│ └─ Centralized policy (e.g., global credit limits) face CRB  │
│                                                               │
│ Financial Operations:                                        │
│ ├─ FX operations: CBN approval required; limits on netting    │
│ ├─ Capital ratios: Standalone; separate from group           │
│ ├─ Loans to group: Restricted (insider lending rules)         │
│ ├─ Dividend repatriation: CBN approval; FX controls applied   │
│ └─ Implication: Cash-flow centralization not possible         │
│                                                               │
│ Technology & Systems:                                        │
│ ├─ Core banking system: Can be upgraded IF independent        │
│ ├─ Data residency: Nigerian data must stay in Nigeria         │
│ ├─ CBN monitoring: Real-time access to all systems required   │
│ ├─ Risk: Off-shoring tech to group data centers = violation   │
│ └─ Implication: Separate systems or expensive local mirror    │
│                                                               │
│ Timeline & Process:                                          │
│ ├─ Acquisition approval: 6–12 months (CBN review)             │
│ ├─ Post-acquisition restructuring: Documented separately      │
│ ├─ Major changes (board, systems, credit policy): 30–90 days  │
│ └─ Implication: Slow integration; regulatory pace            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Competitive Reality in Nigeria:**
- **Market size:** 220M population; ~$400B banking sector (largest in Africa)
- **Consolidation pressure:** CBN merged weak banks in 2020s; larger banks dominate
- **Customer base:** Highly price-sensitive; strong brand loyalty (Tier-1 banks dominate)
- **Management risk:** Acquiring MD and regional heads critical; high poaching risk
- **Integration win:** Cost synergies modest (10–15%) because operations are local-intensive

---

#### **Kenya (Central Bank of Kenya—CBK)**

```
REGULATORY CONSTRAINTS (More Flexible Than Nigeria)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Ownership Structure:                                          │
│ ├─ Foreign ownership: 100% allowed (but CBK watches)          │
│ ├─ No local-ownership minimum (unlike Nigeria)                │
│ ├─ Foreign company CAN own 100% subsidiary                    │
│ ├─ BUT: Subsidiary remains independent (not consolidated)     │
│ └─ Status: Can be 100% owned; cannot be merged into parent    │
│                                                               │
│ Management Control (More Flexible):                          │
│ ├─ Managing Director: CAN be expatriate (with CBK approval)   │
│ ├─ Board chair: Preferred to be Kenyan, but not mandatory     │
│ ├─ Day-to-day policies: More centralization allowed           │
│ ├─ Implication: Group can install global MD; local board OK   │
│ └─ Risk: Perceived foreign control may trigger CBK scrutiny   │
│                                                               │
│ Financial Operations:                                        │
│ ├─ Capital ratios: Standalone, but some group relief allowed  │
│ ├─ Intra-group loans: Allowed (with CBK notification)         │
│ ├─ FX operations: More freedom than Nigeria; less CBN-style   │
│ ├─ Dividend repatriation: More liberal (but KES monitoring)   │
│ └─ Implication: Some cash-flow centralization possible        │
│                                                               │
│ Technology & Systems:                                        │
│ ├─ Core banking system: Can be regional system (not Nigeria)  │
│ ├─ Data residency: Kenya-based backup required; primary OK    │
│ ├─ Implication: Shared platform possible (Kenya + Tanzania)   │
│ └─ Risk: CBK wants audit trail; cannot fully hide systems     │
│                                                               │
│ Timeline & Process:                                          │
│ ├─ Acquisition approval: 3–6 months (faster than Nigeria)     │
│ ├─ Post-acquisition changes: 90–180 days (more flexible)      │
│ ├─ Implication: Faster integration window                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Competitive Reality in Kenya:**
- **Market size:** 54M population; ~$150B banking sector (second in East Africa)
- **Competition:** Tier-1 banks (Equity, KCB, Standard Chartered) dominate; new entrants struggle
- **Customer base:** M-Pesa ecosystem changing banking behavior; digitalization high
- **Technology window:** Kenya more amenable to tech consolidation than Nigeria/Morocco
- **Management risk:** Moderate (Nairobi has tech talent; some poaching risk)
- **Integration win:** Higher (15–25%) because operations support digitalization play

---

#### **Morocco (Bank Al-Maghrib—BAM, plus OCP/Capital Requirements)**

```
REGULATORY CONSTRAINTS (Francophone, EU-influenced)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Ownership Structure:                                          │
│ ├─ Foreign ownership: Maximum 49% (Islamic banking rules)     │
│ ├─ Moroccan ownership: Minimum 51% (non-negotiable)           │
│ ├─ Implication: Foreign buyer cannot become majority owner    │
│ ├─ STRATEGIC CHOICE: Buy Moroccan partner or minority stake   │
│ └─ Status: Cannot control like Nigeria/Kenya acquisitions     │
│                                                               │
│ If Minority Stake (Foreign = 49%):                           │
│ ├─ Board seats: Limited (proportional to ownership)           │
│ ├─ Management: Local partner controls; foreign has veto on    │
│ │  capital, major investments, related-party transactions     │
│ ├─ Integration: Limited (partner will resist centralization)  │
│ └─ Implication: JV dynamics; not full control                 │
│                                                               │
│ Management Control:                                          │
│ ├─ CEO/MD: BAM prefers Moroccan national (not required)       │
│ ├─ Board chair: Moroccan national (near-requirement)          │
│ ├─ Compliance officer: Moroccan national (BAM requirement)    │
│ ├─ Implication: Significant local autonomy                    │
│ └─ Risk: Foreign-imposed decisions trigger regulatory scrutiny│
│                                                               │
│ Financial Operations:                                        │
│ ├─ Capital ratios: IFRS; aligned with EU (for some banks)     │
│ ├─ Credit policy: BAM enforces macro-prudential limits        │
│ ├─ Intra-group loans: Allowed but monitored closely           │
│ ├─ Dividend: Requires BAM approval (especially if foreign)    │
│ └─ Implication: Moderate flexibility; not like Kenya          │
│                                                               │
│ Technology & Systems:                                        │
│ ├─ Core banking system: Can be MENA-regional (Cairn, Gulf)    │
│ ├─ Data residency: Morocco (strict; EU-influenced GDPR view)  │
│ ├─ Compliance: Must use BAM-approved audit vendors            │
│ └─ Implication: Own systems or licensed local partnership     │
│                                                               │
│ Timeline & Process:                                          │
│ ├─ Acquisition approval: 9–18 months (French-style process)   │
│ ├─ Post-acq changes: 180–365 days (lengthy board consultation)
│ └─ Implication: Slowest approval path                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Competitive Reality in Morocco:**
- **Market size:** 37M population; ~$120B banking sector (smallest of three)
- **Competition:** Dominated by legacy banks (BMCE, Attijariwafa Bank); fewer Tier-2 entrants
- **Strategic importance:** Gateway to North Africa + French-speaking Africa
- **Customer base:** French-speaking; relationship-banking (less price-sensitive than West Africa)
- **Management risk:** Moderate (French/North African talent network; less poaching from Lagos/Nairobi)
- **Integration win:** Lower (10–15%) because regulatory constraints limit centralization

---

### B. Regulatory Integration Risk Matrix

```
DIMENSION                 NIGERIA       KENYA         MOROCCO
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Ownership Control         LOWEST        HIGHEST       MEDIUM (49% max)
Local Board Veto          YES (40%)     NO            YES (51% partner)
Management Independence   MUST-LOCAL    FLEXIBLE      MUST-LOCAL
Consolidated Balance      NO            NO            NO
FX Operations Central.    BLOCKED       ALLOWED       RESTRICTED
Tech Consolidation        RISKY         FEASIBLE      RISKY
M&A Approval Speed        SLOWEST       FAST          MEDIUM-SLOW
Dividend Repatriation     RESTRICTED    LIBERAL       MODERATE
Cost Synergy Potential    LOW-MEDIUM    MEDIUM-HIGH   LOW
Regulatory Change Risk    MEDIUM        LOW           MEDIUM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INTEGRATION RISK RATING   HIGH          MEDIUM        MEDIUM-HIGH
```

**Key Insight:** **Nigeria is least consolidatable; Kenya most; Morocco blocked by ownership rules.**

---

## Part II: The Integration Sequencing Strategy

### A. Phase 1: Regulatory & Ownership Clarification (Months 1–6 Post-Close)

**Goal:** Secure unambiguous regulatory approval; establish governance clarity before any operational changes.

#### 1. **Nigeria Regulatory Engagement**

```
IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (First 30 Days Post-Close)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. CBN Board & Senior Management Meeting                      │
│    ├─ Brief: Group's vision; commitment to Nigeria            │
│    ├─ Clarify: This is NIGERIAN bank, growing; not foreign    │
│    │  takeover of Nigerian asset                              │
│    ├─ Document: Commitment to 40% local ownership structure   │
│    ├─ Ask: What does CBN need to see for quick approval?      │
│    └─ Outcome: CBN letter confirming standalone subsidiary    │
│       structure (not consolidated into group)                 │
│                                                               │
│ 2. Local Nigerian Partnership                                 │
│    ├─ Identify: Prominent Nigerian shareholders (40%+ anchor) │
│    ├─ Examples: Aliko Dangote group; Wema Bank legacy families│
│    ├─ Rationale: Shows Nigeria ownership is genuine, not proxy
│    ├─ Structure: Local holding company (40%) + Group (60%)    │
│    └─ Outcome: CBN comfort that ownership rules met           │
│                                                               │
│ 3. Announce to Staff & Customers                              │
│    ├─ Message: "Same bank you know; stronger with group       │
│    │  backing; Nigerian leadership continues"                │
│    ├─ Highlight: Nigerian MD, CFO, board stay/promoted        │
│    ├─ Promise: No branch closures for 3 years                 │
│    └─ Outcome: Retention of key talent; customer confidence  │
│                                                               │
│ 4. Regulatory Submissions (30–90 days)                        │
│    ├─ CBN Filing: Ownership structure diagram; governance     │
│    ├─ CBN Filing: 3-year integration plan (shows independence)│
│    ├─ CBN Filing: Risk management; credit policy framework    │
│    ├─ CBN Filing: Reassurance on data residency              │
│    └─ Outcome: CBN approval (typically 60–90 days)            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PARALLEL: Kenya & Morocco
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ KENYA (Faster Track):                                         │
│ ├─ CBK meeting: Confirm 100%-owned subsidiary allowed        │
│ ├─ CBK filing: Governance; MD appointment (if expat)         │
│ ├─ Timeline: 60 days typical                                 │
│ └─ Advantage: Can move faster than Nigeria/Morocco           │
│                                                               │
│ MOROCCO (Slowest; Different Approach):                        │
│ ├─ If Minority Stake (49%):                                  │
│ │  └─ Identify Moroccan partner (51%); negotiate JV terms     │
│ │  └─ BAM filing: JV agreement; governance; risk management  │
│ │  └─ Timeline: 9–18 months (longer process)                 │
│ │  └─ Implication: Morocco integration delayed till Year 2    │
│ │                                                              │
│ └─ If Majority Ownership Impossible:                          │
│    └─ Contingency: Pivot to strategic partnership (not acq.)  │
│    └─ Example: Distribution partnership; tech services deal   │
│    └─ Implication: Reconsider Morocco as core acquisition    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 2. **Governance Clarity: Board & Management Structure**

```
COUNTRY-SPECIFIC GOVERNANCE SETUP (Post-Regulatory Approval)

NIGERIA (Most Constrained)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Board Composition:                                            │
│ ├─ 9 Board seats (example):                                  │
│ │  ├─ 4 seats: Nigerian shareholders (40% ownership)          │
│ │  ├─ 3 seats: Group-nominated (60% ownership)                │
│ │  ├─ 1 seat: Independent director (Nigerian national)        │
│ │  ├─ 1 seat: CBN-liaison (relationship management)           │
│ │  └─ Chair: Nigerian majority-shareholder (critical)         │
│ │                                                              │
│ ├─ Key Committees:                                           │
│ │  ├─ Audit: Lead by independent director; reports to CBN     │
│ │  ├─ Credit: Lead by Nigerian member; approves >$10M loans   │
│ │  ├─ Risk: Nigerian CRO; reports to board + CBN              │
│ │  └─ Compensation: Nigerian members; vetted by CBN           │
│ │                                                              │
│ │ Management Layer:                                           │
│ ├─ MD/CEO: Nigerian national (non-negotiable)                 │
│ ├─ Reporting line: To board + secondary line to Group COO     │
│ ├─ Key decisions (>N₅B):                                      │
│ │  ├─ Require board approval (not group CEO sign-off)         │
│ │  └─ CRO/board have final say on credit policy              │
│ │                                                              │
│ ├─ CFO: Can be expat (for group systems integration)          │
│ ├─ CRO: Must be Nigerian national                             │
│ ├─ COO: Can be expat (back-office optimization)               │
│ └─ HR: Local hiring; local benefits; not group-harmonized     │
│                                                               │
│ Autonomy Protected:                                          │
│ ├─ Credit policy: Set by Nigerian board + CBN guidance        │
│ ├─ Branch network: No closures without board + CBN approval   │
│ ├─ Major technology: Nigerian CRO approval required           │
│ ├─ Dividend: CBN approval; not automatic group sweep          │
│ └─ Implication: Real independence; not holding-company puppet │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

KENYA (Moderate Constraints)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Board Composition:                                            │
│ ├─ 7 Board seats (example):                                  │
│ │  ├─ 3 seats: Group-nominated (full control)                │
│ │  ├─ 2 seats: Local partners/minority shareholders           │
│ │  ├─ 1 seat: Independent director (Kenyan preferred)         │
│ │  └─ Chair: Group-nominated (CAN be expat)                   │
│ │                                                              │
│ │ Management Layer:                                           │
│ ├─ MD/CEO: CAN be expat (with CBK approval)                   │
│ ├─ Reporting: Primarily to Group; secondary to board          │
│ ├─ Key decisions (>KES 5B):                                   │
│ │  ├─ May be made by group CEO + regional MD (faster)         │
│ │  └─ Board approval still required (governance)              │
│ │                                                              │
│ ├─ CFO: Likely expat (for group consolidation)                │
│ ├─ CRO: Can be expat; reports to group CRO + local board      │
│ ├─ COO: Expat (opportunity for shared services with Tanzania)  │
│ └─ HR: Some localization; benefits can be region-aligned      │
│                                                               │
│ Autonomy Reduced (Compared to Nigeria):                       │
│ ├─ Credit policy: More group influence; less board veto       │
│ ├─ Branch decisions: Faster (less regulatory friction)        │
│ ├─ Technology: Can be regional (Kenya + Tanzania shared)      │
│ ├─ Dividend: Faster repatriation (less FX control)            │
│ └─ Implication: Faster integration possible; still subsidiary │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MOROCCO (Depends on Structure)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ IF Minority Stake (49%) with Moroccan Partner (51%):         │
│ ├─ Board (7 seats, example):                                 │
│ │  ├─ 3 seats: Moroccan partner                               │
│ │  ├─ 2 seats: Group-nominated                                │
│ │  ├─ 1 seat: Independent (Moroccan national)                 │
│ │  └─ Chair: Moroccan partner (controls agenda)               │
│ │                                                              │
│ │ Management Layer:                                           │
│ ├─ MD: Moroccan national (partner controls)                   │
│ ├─ CFO: May be expat (minority right; limited veto)           │
│ ├─ CRO: Moroccan national (partner controls)                  │
│ ├─ Implication: Limited integration; JV dynamics             │
│ └─ Risk: Partner will resist many centralizations             │
│                                                               │
│ IF Cannot Achieve Ownership: PIVOT STRATEGY                  │
│ ├─ Option A: Joint venture with Moroccan bank (technology    │
│ │  sharing; distribution partnership)                         │
│ ├─ Option B: Partner with Moroccan fintech (enter market via  │
│ │  tech stack, not acquisition)                               │
│ ├─ Option C: Defer Morocco for 3–5 years (focus Nigeria/Kenya)
│ └─ Implication: Morocco not primary integration target        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### B. Phase 2: Brand & Customer Communication (Months 3–9 Post-Close)

**Goal:** Communicate changes transparently to prevent customer/employee defection; build confidence in new ownership.

#### 1. **Brand Architecture Decision Matrix**

```
DECISION POINT 1: Single Global Brand vs. Local Brands?

SINGLE GLOBAL BRAND (One logo, "Group Banking Services")
├─ Pros:
│  ├─ Cost efficient (single marketing; brand awareness)
│  ├─ Institutional credibility (signals scale)
│  └─ Easier cross-sell ("bring your savings to Group")
│
├─ Cons:
│  ├─ Customer churn risk (lose local loyalty; "lost my bank")
│  ├─ Regulatory risk (CBN/BAM may see as "foreign control")
│  ├─ Management talent flight ("bank I worked for disappeared")
│  └─ Brand value loss (especially if global brand is weak vs. local)
│
└─ RECOMMENDATION: NOT for Nigeria/Morocco; risky

LOCAL BRANDS RETAINED (Nigeria Bank, Kenya Bank, Morocco Bank)
├─ Pros:
│  ├─ Customer loyalty protected (same name they know)
│  ├─ Regulatory comfort ("it's still Nigerian bank")
│  ├─ Management retention (pride in local brand)
│  ├─ Speed of integration (no customer re-onboarding)
│  └─ Flexibility (each brand can evolve locally)
│
├─ Cons:
│  ├─ Higher marketing costs (three campaigns)
│  ├─ Brand awareness of Group is weak (not "household name")
│  ├─ Less cross-selling efficiency
│  └─ IT costs (maintain brand-differentiation systems)
│
└─ RECOMMENDATION: YES for Nigeria/Morocco; conditional for Kenya

HYBRID: "LOCAL BANK, PART OF GROUP" (Recommended)
├─ Tier-1 Brand: Local name (unchanged) — on all customer materials
├─ Tier-2 Brand: "Part of [Group Name]" (small, secondary)
│  └─ Example: "ABC Bank (A Group Banking Services company)"
│  └─ Positioning: "Same bank. Stronger support. Same service."
│
├─ Pros:
│  ├─ Customer loyalty protected (primary identity = local)
│  ├─ Group brand visibility grows (slowly; not threatening)
│  ├─ Regulatory comfort (local bank is clearly in control)
│  ├─ Management retention (local brand pride maintained)
│  ├─ Cost efficiency (some shared brand guidelines)
│  └─ Cross-selling possible ("Group benefits": lower rates, etc.)
│
├─ Cons:
│  ├─ Moderate brand-management complexity
│  ├─ Group brand awareness still limited (requires time)
│  └─ Some IT costs (two-tier branding in systems)
│
└─ RECOMMENDATION: ADOPT FOR ALL THREE MARKETS

THREE-MARKET BRANDING ROADMAP
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ YEAR 1: Local Brands Protect Identity                        │
│ ├─ Nigeria: "ABC Bank Nigeria (A Group Banking Services Co.)"│
│ ├─ Kenya: "ABC Bank Kenya (A Group Banking Services Co.)"    │
│ ├─ Morocco: "ABC Maroc (A Group Banking Services Co.)"        │
│ ├─ Communication: "Celebrating 40 years in [country]"        │
│ │            "Now with global backing for better service"    │
│ └─ Outcome: Customer continuity; brand transition begun      │
│                                                               │
│ YEAR 2-3: Group Services Highlighted                         │
│ ├─ Secondary brand lift: "A Group Banking Services Network"  │
│ ├─ New campaigns highlight: Cross-border products            │
│ │  "Send money to Kenya without leaving Nigeria"             │
│ ├─ Benefits narrative: "Same service; Group pricing power"   │
│ └─ Outcome: Group awareness grows; local pride maintained    │
│                                                               │
│ YEAR 3+: Consolidation Option (If Appetite)                  │
│ ├─ Possibility: Unified brand (if regulatory permits +        │
│ │  customer surveys show acceptance)                          │
│ ├─ Alternative: Co-branding permanently ("ABC Group, locally  │
│ │  present in [countries]")                                  │
│ └─ Outcome: Strategic optionality; not forced now             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 2. **Customer Communication Plan (First 90 Days)**

```
COMMUNICATION CASCADE (Months 1–3 Post-Close)

WEEK 1: External Announcement
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Message (Consistent Across Markets):                         │
│ "ABC Bank Group is acquiring [Local Bank Name]. This is      │
│  growth for the bank, not a takeover. You will continue to   │
│  bank with us under the same name, with the same service,    │
│  and the same commitment to [country name] and our customers."│
│                                                               │
│ Key Points (Localized):                                      │
│ ├─ Local bank identity protected                             │
│ ├─ Local leadership team continues (MD name + photo)         │
│ ├─ No branch closures planned (for minimum 3 years)          │
│ ├─ Local employment unaffected                               │
│ ├─ Better service via Group resources (faster loans,         │
│ │  technology, lower costs)                                  │
│ ├─ Regulatory approval being sought (implies care, not speed)│
│ └─ Questions? [Local contact number, not Group HQ]           │
│                                                               │
│ Channels:                                                    │
│ ├─ Press conference (local media; in-language)               │
│ ├─ Email to all customers ("your bank is growing")           │
│ ├─ Branch posters (before news breaks)                       │
│ ├─ Social media (local language; local MD introduces change) │
│ └─ CEO/MD video message (personal; builds trust)             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MONTH 1: Customer Assurance Campaign
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Channels & Messages:                                         │
│ ├─ Email campaign (weekly): "What's changing; what's not"   │
│ │  Week 1: "Your account numbers stay the same"              │
│ │  Week 2: "Your branch is not closing"                      │
│ │  Week 3: "Your relationship manager is same person"        │
│ │  Week 4: "New capabilities coming (better rates, etc.)"    │
│ │                                                              │
│ ├─ Branch events: Coffee & conversation (local MD + managers)│
│ │  Topic: "Ask us anything; we're same bank, now stronger"   │
│ │  Attendance: High-risk segments (large depositors,          │
│ │  relationship accounts)                                     │
│ │                                                              │
│ ├─ Customer service training: All frontline (tellers, phone) │
│ │  Message: "Same service; now backed by larger group"       │
│ │  Script: "What part of your banking experience would       │
│ │  improve if we could do X, Y, Z faster?"                   │
│ │                                                              │
│ └─ Website update:                                           │
│     ├─ FAQ section: "Will you close my account? No."        │
│     ├─ Group overview (subdomain; not primary)               │
│     ├─ New features coming (e.g., "cross-border payments")  │
